prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Reading the eight openings, B042 is the only candidate that every one of us ranked, with five of eight in the top two or three, and I do not want to confuse that breadth with merit. So I checked it on its own terms. The magic-wavelength lattice is a simple image with large consequences: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift is the same for both clock states, and thousands of atoms can be held for long times without Doppler or recoil shifts, while the clock transition is left undisturbed. That is a discovery about how to make an atom a clean quantum system, not an engineering refinement. The result is that the lattice clock reaches fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, the comparison of clocks at millimetre height differences shows the gravitational redshift in the laboratory, and constraints on varying constants and dark-matter couplings follow. The field is also the kind I value most: results reproduced and compared at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and elsewhere, with theory and experiment in close agreement and the uncertainty budgets understood. Attribution is compact: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for bringing the strontium clock to the accuracy and stability frontier and for the link to the frequency comb. Two laureates is a fair, defensible allocation.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterargument is novelty. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control and clocks) have already been recognised on neighbouring ground, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks a successor step rather than a new discovery. The credit also leaves out other contributors to the lattice-clock story (early theory on magic wavelengths, ytterbium and other strontium groups, and the SYRTE and PTB work), and some of the headline payoffs, the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy, are still pending rather than delivered. If the committee wants a prize that tells us something new about the boundary between quantum and classical worlds, B042 is less dramatic than some others, because it is a measurement achievement and its fundamental physics results so far are null results.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B042 only fifth and raised the overlap with the 2012 prize on measuring and manipulating single quantum systems, together with the question of whether Ye's other contributions blur the attribution of the lattice-clock concept.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but I think it is smaller than it looks. The 2012 work is about trapped single ions, where the motional problem is solved by a different route (a Paul trap, laser cooling of one ion, quantum logic spectroscopy). The lattice clock solves it for a large ensemble by the magic wavelength, and it gets its statistical advantage from the number of atoms, which is a distinct physical idea. On Ye, the concept belongs to Katori; Ye's decisive contribution is bringing it to record accuracy and stability, including the many-body regime. I would say that in the citation so the claim does not drift into a generic 'clocks' prize. I would also point out that Danielsson himself puts B042 in the top five, so we may disagree more about the ranking than about the validity.

responses.point: Mehlig placed B007 first on the strength of a clean, general mechanism (the Z2 invariant and protected edge states) with a decisive experimental realisation, and placed B042 only eighth, citing adjacency to the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the fact that its impact beyond metrology is still prospective.
responses.response: I agree that the topological classification is a deep idea and I rank it third myself, but I want to qualify the claim that its attribution is clean. Mehlig acknowledges that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu are outside the credited names, and I would add Hasan and Moore for the three-dimensional case. For me this is a real obstacle: the three names would leave a dispute that this list cannot settle, and I would not want to choose a trio on that basis. The 2016 prize also covers part of the conceptual ground. Against that, lattice clocks have a short and well-documented attribution chain. On impact beyond metrology, measurement is the point: relativistic redshift at the millimetre scale is already a result outside what a clock was built for. I accept that the case for B007 would improve if colleagues with more condensed-matter expertise than mine can settle the credit.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B056 first, argued that aberration-corrected electron optics is a mature, overdue instrument that opened a door, and said that the relation of B042 to earlier frequency metrology prizes could lead some to see it as incremental.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson on the general principle that an instrument which opens a new regime can be a Nobel-worthy discovery, and the same argument supports B042. I do not agree that the clock is incremental: Hall and Hansch gave us the comb that makes optical frequencies countable, but the lattice clock is what turned that into a standard better than caesium by several orders of magnitude. I would be the first to say that in B056 the question is a physics-versus-instrumentation balance, and Olsson herself flags her bias as a microscopist. I defer to her on the priority question between Rose, Haider and Urban and the parallel STEM-corrector work, but I do not find that the supplied evidence raises it above the lattice clock.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B029 first as a new observational window built on a detector concept, and ranked B042 second, saying it is mature, extensively confirmed and well aligned with the metrology tradition of the prize.
responses.response: I agree with the second ranking and I am glad to see support from outside atomic physics. On B029 I would ask whether the discovery is firm enough on the source side: the diffuse flux is solid, but Pearce himself notes that individual sources are still few and the origin of most of the flux is unresolved. I also share his concern on credit in a very large collaboration with AMANDA and Baikal predecessors. This is a difficult attribution for a two-person prize. For my part, I defer to Pearce and Danielsson on particle and astroparticle questions, so if they argue the credit is defensible I would want to hear the evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or sees them as a successor step.
Whether a third contributor (an early lattice-clock theory or ytterbium group) should be credited, which the supplied names do not settle.
I have not independently checked the latest accuracy and stability figures.
If the committee prefers B010, the split among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger remains unresolved and a three-person limit forces a hard choice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B042 or the alternatives. Katori and Ye are not named among my collaborators. I do collaborate closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and her Lund group, but that is outside the shortlisted ballots; I also note the atomic-theory community is small and I would recuse myself if a closer tie to a candidate emerges.
